drills.q: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list. State the algorithm and complexity.
drills.a: Min-heap seeded with each list's head; pop smallest, append to output, push its .next if present. O(N log K) time, O(K) space.

drills.q: Why is O(N log K) better than the naive O(NK) approach, and what does the naive approach actually do wrong?
drills.a: The naive approach scans all K current heads to find the minimum at every step (O(K) per output element, O(NK) total); the heap finds the minimum in O(log K) instead since it never holds more than K elements.

drills.q: Find the kth smallest element in an n x n matrix sorted ascending by row and column, using the k-way merge idea.
drills.a: Treat each row as one sorted sequence; heap seeded with (value, row, col=0) for every row; pop k times, pushing each row's next element after its current head is popped.

drills.q: Find the smallest range that includes at least one element from each of k sorted lists. What do you track besides the heap, and when do you stop?
drills.a: Track a running current-maximum (O(1) variable) alongside the heap minimum; check the range at every pop; stop the moment any single list is exhausted since it can no longer produce a new minimum.

drills.q: You need to merge k sorted arrays too large to fit in memory. How does the algorithm change?
drills.a: Same heap-of-heads logic, but each sequence becomes a buffered read cursor into a file; when a sequence's in-memory buffer empties, refill it from disk. This is how external merge sort and LSM-tree SSTable compaction work.

drills.q: You only need the top-N results from merging k sorted result sets (a paginated query), not the full merge. How do you optimize?
drills.a: Use the same heap but stop after N pops instead of exhausting every sequence — the early-termination variant shared with the Top-K pattern.
